newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Canadian miner waged last cash for gold.
newsitem.headline: Canadian miner waged last cash for gold.

text.p: (Note: all dollar amounts in U.S. unless stated otherwise)
By K.T. Arasu

Maverick Canadian miner David Walsh spent the last Canadian $10,000 ($7,425) that Bre-X Minerals Ltd. had in the bank on a trip to Indonesia in April 1993, a gamble that landed him one of the world's largest gold finds.

"At that time Bre-X was down to its last C$10,000, which I spent on coming over here. There's nothing like success. Our other explorations have been zero. I had never imagined it would be this big," Walsh said in an interview in Jakarta.
Bre-X found the Busang property in East Kalimantan province on Borneo Island, estimated by Bre-X to contain at least 57 million ounces of gold currently worth over $21 billion.
"Whatever personal success that has come out of this, I haven't had a chance to enjoy it. It's been extremely hard work the last four years," he said.

Bre-X and Walsh's troubles began late last year when the Indonesian government ordered the company to form a partnership with Barrick Gold Corp. of Canada to exploit Busang. The government also wanted a 10-percent share of the deposit.
The two companies, in a joint submission to the Mines and Energy Ministry, last December agreed to split the property 67.5 percent for Barrick, 22.5 percent for Bre-X and the rest to the government.
Since then, Indonesian timber baron Muhammad "Bob" Hasan, a close associate of President Suharto, has entered the picture.

The Nusamba Group, 80-percent owned by three foundations which Suharto heads and 10 percent each by Hasan and the president's oldest son Sigit Harjojudanto, has bought 50 percent stakes in two Bre-X partner companies that each have a 10-percent interest in the two richest parts of the property.
Waiting in the wings is another Canadian mining firm, Placer Dome Inc., which has proposed a $5 billion merger with Bre-X under which Indonesian interests would get a 40-percent stake in Busang.
Bre-X also faces a C$2 billion ($1.49 billion) lawsuit filed in Canada by Indonesian businessman Jusuf Merukh, who claims to own 40 percent of the property.
The Indonesian government has given Bre-X and Barrick until Feb. 14 to reach an agreement with their respective local partners. Walsh says he expects Bre-X to settle in the coming week.
Bre-X, meanwhile, dismisses the claim by Merukh, who has an undisputed 10-percent stake in the central Busang zone estimated to contain about three million ounces of gold, as without merit.
"If we have to do it over again, we certainly would have built stronger relationships in Indonesia...which we are doing now. I don't believe it's too late," Walsh said.

Industry sources said Walsh's personal share of Busang from his stake in Bre-X would have totalled $1.5 billion if the company had picked its own partner to develop the find, but Walsh dismissed this as speculation.
"It's definitely not $1.5 billion. I had probably a 35 or 40 percent stake in Bre-X. When people ask me how much I now have in Bre-X, I say not enough," he said with a laugh.
Dressed casually in a beige short-sleeved shirt and matching pants, Walsh, 51, recounted how his instincts and courage to take risks paid off where others had failed.

"Nineteen previous holes were drilled in the central zone (of Busang) that were incorrect," he said. "When a company decided to pull out because it was quiet there, we decided to take the contrary view."

Walsh said PT Westralian Atan Minerals (PT WAM) chose to sell its option on the central zone for $80,000. "I had no money but a commitment...that I would finance the exploration and acquisition of Busang I (the central zone)," he said.
"Bre-X was a shell of a company then, with virtually no working capital," he said.

Walsh said he raised the money by selling his Bre-X stock options at various prices -- 10 to 15 Canadian cents (7.4 cents to 11.1 cents) in 1993, compared with well over C$200 ($148.50) before a 10-for-one share split in May last year.
"I convinced some of my friends and business associates to buy the shares," he said.
"Further drilling showed mineralisation extended into the southeastern zone (Busang II)," he said.
Walsh's partner Askatindo Karya Mineral had a mining permit for Busang II -- and this is where they hit real pay dirt over the past 18 months. This zone holds the bulk of the motherlode.

Walsh said he initially thought the gold deposit would amount to some one million ounces and be confined to the central zone. "We were shooting for one or two, possibily three million ounces as we kept drilling," he said.

"I figured that when we started this, two or three million ounces in the central zone...some major company would buy us out (at) C$3-C$4-C$5 ($2.23 to $3.71) a share and (I) will go for a vacation on the beach. But that's not the way it turned out...," he said.
